description:
Hi everyone! We are a team of six participants from Lahore, Pakistan, taking part in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

We are interested in Computer Science, web development, AI/ML, space exploration, and solving real-world problems using NASA's open data. Our goal is to collaborate, learn from one another, and build an innovative project that combines technology with space science
summary:
MARS ECHO is a web-based Mars mission-planning workstation that helps astronauts and planners decide where a spacewalk can safely go and whether the crew can get back. We built an interactive Mars map and added four connected tools: a terrain risk map, an EVA resource monitor, a route planner, and a return-feasibility check.

Using real NASA MGS MOLA elevation data (PDS4), the app calculates the slope of every map cell and rates it Easy, Moderate, Difficult, or Very Difficult. It then uses A* pathfinding to plan outbound and return routes under three strategies (Shortest, Lowest Risk, and Balanced). For each route it estimates walking time and oxygen, battery, and cooling use, and gives a clear verdict: Feasible, At Risk, or Not Feasible, with the limiting resource named.

This matters because a Mars crew has finite life support, and the wrong route can be unsafe. MARS ECHO puts terrain risk and return planning in one place so decisions can be made before the first step. Resource rates are simulated assumptions, not real NASA suit telemetry.

details:
What it does
MARS ECHO is a web-based Mars mission-planning workstation. It lets a planner explore the Martian surface, see how dangerous the terrain is, track an astronaut’s life-support resources, and plan a walking route that can get the crew back to the habitat safely.

How it works

  1. Mars Explorer: An interactive map of Mars with switchable layers (orbital imagery, elevation, hillshade, geology), coordinate and site search, and markers for habitats, rovers, astronauts, and science sites. The default view is Jezero Crater.
  2. Terrain Risk Map: The app loads real NASA MGS MOLA elevation grids from the PDS4 archive, calculates the slope of every cell, and classes it as Easy, Moderate, Difficult, or Very Difficult. The thresholds are adjustable.
  3. EVA Resource Monitor: A simulation of oxygen, battery, cooling, and mission time, with Normal, Warning, Critical, and Depleted states, a consumption chart, and a return reserve estimator.
  4. Return Path Optimizer: The user sets a habitat and a destination. A* pathfinding over the terrain grid plans outbound and return routes under three strategies (Shortest, Lowest Risk, and Balanced). The app then estimates walking time, accounting for slope, and the extra resource use on hard terrain. Each route gets a verdict of Feasible, At Risk, or Not Feasible against a safety reserve, along with the limiting resource and a plain-language explanation.

Benefits and intended impact
Planners can compare routes and see return risk before a crew leaves the habitat, in one tool rather than several. It also works as an educational tool for showing how terrain and life support limit Mars exploration. The same approach could extend to the Moon.

Tools and technologies
React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, OpenLayers (map engine), Lucide icons, SVG charts, and a backend service that reads NASA PDS4 MOLA data. Data: NASA MGS MOLA topography (bundle DOI 10.17189/1z1b-kv84) and NASA/USGS orbital map layers.

What makes it creative
It combines three things that are usually separate: a planetary GIS viewer, a terrain hazard model, and a life-support feasibility check. The question it answers is not “what does Mars look like?” but “can the astronaut get there and get back alive?”

Factors we considered

  • Data integrity: The app never fabricates elevation data. If NASA data fails to load, it says so. A synthetic test mode is clearly labeled as not real data.
  • Honesty about limits: Terrain analysis uses large-scale slope only (463 to 926 m per pixel) and cannot detect rocks or small craters. Resource rates are simulated planning assumptions, not real NASA suit telemetry.
  • Accessibility: Status is shown with icons and text labels, not color alone.
  • Adjustability: Thresholds, resource profiles, and route rules can be changed by the user.
  • Future work: Real telemetry, higher-resolution elevation, and hazard layers such as dust and radiation.
